newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia CPI moderation to continue.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST-Australia CPI moderation to continue.

text.p: One of the big surprises of the Australian economy in 1996 was the rapid improvement in inflation, an improvement that allowed interest rates to be cut three times in five months to stimulate the slowing economy.
Further evidence of the improvement is expected on Wednesday when December quarter inflation data are released. The figures are expected to leave open the chance of another rate cut.
Economists expect the key underlying rate to have fallen to the lower end of the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) target band, and see it dipping even lower in the first half of 1997.
"Low inflation will be entrenched in Australia until mid-1998," Colonial State Bank economists said in a report.
Forecasts of economists surveyed by Reuters centre on a 0.4 percent rise in the underlying rate, leading to an annual rate of 2.1 percent. Annual forecasts range from 1.9 to 2.3 percent.
The underlying rate removes many of the volatile and seasonal items from the CPI, such as mortgage charges, to give a truer picture of supply and demand forces in the economy.
The RBA targets the underlying rate, aiming to keep it to an average of two and three percent over a run of years.

And with partial price indicators remaining restrained and wages growth still moderate, economists expect the underlying rate to remain comfortably with the bottom half of the RBA's band through 1997.

The consumer price index (CPI) is expected to have risen 0.3 percent in the quarter, reflecting the first cut in official interest rates on July 31. That would see the annual rate down at 1.6 percent, with forecasts ranging from 1.5 to 1.9 percent.
The CPI is expected to fall further through 1997, possibly under 1.0 percent, as the impact of the November and December rate cuts feeds through to consumers.
Although the CPI is not targetted by the RBA, economists said it is still important because it is what people outside the financial markets look at when they talk about inflation.

"While the headline CPI is not the focus of the RBA's target, it has an important psychological effect on inflationary expectations, and hence, the wage negotiation and bargaining process," Hambros fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.

Economists said that if the CPI and underlying rate come in as forecast, the chances of a fourth rate cut will improve given that both headline and underlrying rates are expected to moderate further through 1997.

A rate cut could occur even amid some tentative signs of economic growth at the beginning of 1997 if the RBA remains confident of further moderation in price pressures and restrained wages growth, economists said.

ANZ Treasury economists, at the low end of market forecasts for inflation, saw room for the RBA to ease being created by a favourable inflation report. "Such a result could open the door to one last easing in this cycle, given the still positive inflation outlook," they said in a commentary.
